title: "Study B: do the three contraceptive methods differ in vaginal community composition?"

  warning: false

**Where we got to — the story so far.** Three documents, in the order we
made them:

| # | Document | Question | Answer in one line |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `01-qc.qmd` | Is the data good enough to analyse? | Yes — all six files agree; three flags to carry forward |
| 2 | this one | Do the arms differ in community *composition*? | No evidence — arm explains ~3% of distances, p = 0.15; Nugent explains 24% |
| 3 | `03-bv-by-arm.qmd` | Is **BV** more common in one arm? | No evidence — rates 49% / 36% / 38%, p = 0.45 |

This one — the first analysis document, written Wednesday — follows Tuesday's
ordination pipeline: look first, then PERMANOVA, then the checks that stop
the test lying to us. The three arms are `injectable` (39 people), `pill`
(28) and `ring` (26); one sample each, 93 in total. The grouping comes from
the metadata (which method each person was assigned), not from any count
table, so testing the microbiome table against it is fair.

## Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup
source(here::here("R/count_tables.R"))
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(microViz)
  library(phyloseq)
  library(vegan)    # adonis2 (PERMANOVA) and betadisper
  library(dplyr)
  library(ggplot2)
})
set.seed(2026)   # so the permutation p-values are the same on every re-render

# Study B species table. min_count = 1, min_samples = 1 drops the 86 species
# that never appear in any sample — the QC report said to pre-filter those
# before any distance-based analysis.
ps <- as_counts("group_b", table = "microbiome", min_count = 1, min_samples = 1)
ps
```

Every number below starts from these **134 species x 93 samples**.

## The answer first, in plain words

If you only read one section, read this one. Its table is computed from the
data, so the numbers cannot drift from the truth; the sections after it are
the working.

**What the question means.** "Community composition" is which species live
in each sample and how abundant each one is — the whole 134-species profile
at once, not one species at a time. Two people can both have BV and still
differ in composition; two with different BV status almost always do.

**What the test does.** PERMANOVA measures how similar every pair of samples
is (Bray-Curtis distance), then asks: do samples from the same arm sit
closer together than samples from different arms? The **R2** is the share
of all that variation the grouping explains. The **p-value** is how often
chance alone — shuffling the labels — produces a result at least that
strong.

```{r}
#| label: answer-table
# One model, three variables, each tested as if it entered last (by =
# "margin"). dist_ans is the same Bray-Curtis matrix the whole document uses.
meta_ans <- as(sample_data(ps), "data.frame")
dist_ans <- ps |> tax_transform("compositional") |> dist_calc("bray")
ans <- adonis2(dist_ans@dist ~ arm + rnaseq_batch + nugent,
               data = meta_ans, by = "margin", permutations = 999)

tibble(
  variable = c("Arm — which contraceptive method",
               "Sequencing batch",
               "Nugent score — BV severity"),
  `R2 (share of variation explained)` = round(ans$R2[1:3], 3),
  `p-value` = ans[["Pr(>F)"]][1:3]
) |> knitr::kable()
```

**The answer: no evidence the arms differ in composition.** Three reasons,
in the order of how much each matters:

1. **Arm explains almost nothing: about 3%.** In the primary model (arm +
   batch, section 2) it is R2 = 0.033, p = 0.15 — chance produces a 3% R2
   easily. In the three-variable model in the table above (which adds BV
   severity, so arm is tested after BV is accounted for) it is R2 = 0.030,
   p = 0.069 — closer to the boundary, still above 0.05. Both models say
   the same thing.

2. **The same test finds a real signal in the same data.** The Nugent score
   explains **24%** of the distances at p = **0.001**. That is what a true
   difference looks like through this pipeline — so the pipeline works; the
   arm signal just is not there. If contraceptive method had shifted
   composition the way BV does, this table would have shown it.

3. **The answer survives every alternative choice.** A second, completely
   different distance (Aitchison) agrees (R2 = 0.029, p = 0.16). The
   dispersions are equal, so PERMANOVA is not being fooled by one arm being
   more spread out (section 3). The QC flags change nothing (section 7).
   And the shuffle-null (section 6) shows the real R2 sitting in the middle
   of what random labels produce — 4 of 20 shuffles beat it.

**What this study did *not* show.** It did not show the arms have identical
communities — no study can show that. With 93 people, a modest real
difference would have been invisible; only a fairly large one had a chance.
And each person was sampled once, so this compares *between people*, not
change within a person over time.

The sections below show the working: the ordination by eye (1), the test (2),
the dispersion check (3), the second distance (4), what *does* structure the
plot (5), the shuffle-null (6) and the robustness checks (7).

## 1. Look first: the ordination

```{r}
#| label: dist
# Each sample's counts become shares of that sample's total (compositional),
# then Bray-Curtis distance between every pair of samples.
pe <- ps |>
  tax_transform("compositional") |>
  dist_calc("bray")
dist_bray <- pe@dist          # the distance matrix, in the @dist slot
meta <- as(sample_data(ps), "data.frame")
```

```{r}
#| label: ord-arm
pe |> ord_calc("PCoA") |> ord_plot(colour = "arm")
```

The two axes hold most of the structure (33.8% and 26% of the variation), so
this is a fairly complete two-dimensional view. Counting the points: 39
injectable, 28 pill, 26 ring. The three colours are **mixed together** — no
arm occupies its own corner of the plot.

## 2. Test: PERMANOVA

**What it does, in plain sentences:** PERMANOVA takes the distance matrix and
asks, "when I group samples by arm, are samples from the same arm closer to
each other than samples from different arms?" The R² is the share of all the
pairwise variation that the grouping explains. The p-value comes from
shuffling the labels many times and seeing how often a shuffle explains as
much as the real grouping. (This is `adonis2` from
[vegan](https://cran.r-project.org/package=vegan); the method is from Anderson
2001, [*A new method for non-parametric multivariate analysis of
variance*](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0006-341X.2001.00470.x).)

```{r}
#| label: permanova
# by = "margin": each term is tested as if it entered the model last, so
# arm's R2 is what arm explains after accounting for sequencing batch.
perm <- adonis2(dist_bray ~ arm + rnaseq_batch,
               data = meta, by = "margin", permutations = 999)
perm
```

Arm explains **R2 = 0.033, p = 0.15**. Batch explains essentially nothing
(R2 = 0.006, p = 0.68). So the ordination's visual impression and the test
agree: **no evidence the three arms differ in community composition.**

## 3. The catch: are we sure we're comparing centres, not spreads?

PERMANOVA has a known weakness: a small p-value can mean the group *centres*
differ (what we're asking) *or* merely that one group is more spread out than
the others. `betadisper` tests the spread directly, so we check it before
trusting the PERMANOVA verdict.

```{r}
#| label: dispersion
permutest(betadisper(dist_bray, meta$arm), permutations = 999)
permutest(betadisper(dist_bray, meta$rnaseq_batch), permutations = 999)
```

Dispersion is equal across arms (p = 0.76) and batches (p = 0.16). So there is
no spread difference that could masquerade as an arm difference — the "no
difference" verdict stands on clean ground. (If dispersion *had* differed,
the right response would have been to lean on ordination plots and report
both.)

## 4. A second distance, same question

Bray-Curtis is one choice. The Aitchison distance (CLR transform, then
Euclidean) is the compositional-data alternative — it measures differences in
*log-ratios*, which is what compositional data are actually made of. The CLR
transform here handled the zeros by adding half the smallest nonzero count in
the whole table (that smallest count is 2, so it added 1) before taking logs.

```{r}
#| label: aitchison
pe_clr <- ps |> tax_transform("clr") |> dist_calc("euclidean")

adonis2(pe_clr@dist ~ arm + rnaseq_batch,
        data = meta, by = "margin", permutations = 999)

permutest(betadisper(pe_clr@dist, meta$arm), permutations = 999)
pe_clr |> ord_calc("PCoA") |> ord_plot(colour = "arm")
```

Same story from a different angle: R2 = 0.029, p = 0.16, equal dispersion
(p = 0.91), no clustering by arm in the plot.

## 5. What *does* structure the plot

The ordination obviously has structure — axis 1 holds 33.8% of the
variation — it just isn't arm. Let's colour the same Bray-Curtis ordination by
the BV status label (from the Nugent score, in the metadata) and test it the
same way.

```{r}
#| label: what-structures
pe |> ord_calc("PCoA") |> ord_plot(colour = "bv")

adonis2(dist_bray ~ arm + nugent + rnaseq_batch,
        data = meta, by = "margin", permutations = 999)

# BV label and Nugent score, from the metadata, by arm:
table(meta$arm, meta$bv)
fisher.test(table(meta$arm, meta$bv))
kruskal.test(nugent ~ arm, data = meta)
```

This is the contrast that makes the whole report interpretable:

- **Nugent explains R2 = 0.24 of the distances (p = 0.001)** — the community
  composition tracks BV status strongly, as it should.
- **The three arms have similar BV rates** (49% / 36% / 38% positive;
  Fisher p = 0.45, Nugent Kruskal p = 0.63), so what composition varies with
  is present in all three arms at similar rates.
- Even in this model, arm stays non-significant (R2 = 0.030, p = 0.058) —
  borderline, which is worth knowing, but not evidence, especially after
  we've already run two primary tests above it.

## 6. What "no difference" looks like: a shuffle-null

Tuesday's step 5, applied to our question: shuffle the arm labels 20 times,
run PERMANOVA on each, and mark where the real R2 lands.

```{r}
#| label: shuffle-null
real_r2 <- adonis2(dist_bray ~ arm, data = meta, permutations = 999)$R2[1]

shuffled <- sapply(1:20, function(i) {
  meta2 <- meta
  meta2$arm <- sample(meta2$arm)          # arm labels, randomly reassigned
  adonis2(dist_bray ~ arm, data = meta2, permutations = 99)$R2[1]
})

tibble(shuffled) |>
  ggplot(aes(shuffled)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 12, fill = "grey85", colour = "black") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = real_r2, colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Arm R2 vs 20 random shuffles of the arm labels",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Red line = real R2 (", round(real_r2, 3),
      "). Shuffles range ", round(min(shuffled), 3), " to ",
      round(max(shuffled), 3),
      "; ", sum(shuffled >= real_r2), " of 20 shuffles beat it."
    ),
    x = "PERMANOVA R2 for arm"
  )
```

**`r sum(shuffled >= real_r2)` of 20 random shuffles explained as much as the
real arm labels did.** The real R2 sits in the middle of the noise
distribution — that is exactly what "no evidence of a difference" looks like.

## 7. Does the verdict survive the QC flags?

The QC report flagged one shallow sample (`B006`, 5,247 reads) and told us to
pre-filter never-observed species (done in setup). Robustness check:

```{r}
#| label: robustness
# Drop the shallow sample:
keep <- meta$sample_id != "B006"
db2 <- as.dist(as.matrix(dist_bray)[keep, keep])
adonis2(db2 ~ arm + rnaseq_batch,
        data = meta[keep, ], by = "margin", permutations = 999)

# And without any species pre-filter (all 220):
ps0 <- as_counts("group_b", table = "microbiome")
db0 <- ps0 |>
  tax_transform("compositional") |>
  dist_calc("bray") |>
  (\(x) x@dist)()
adonis2(db0 ~ arm, data = meta, permutations = 999)
```

Dropping `B006`: R2 = 0.034, p = 0.11. Keeping all 220 species: R2 = 0.033,
p = 0.15. Neither QC flag changes the verdict.

## Verdict

**No evidence that the three contraceptive methods differ in vaginal
community composition.** Arm explains about 3% of the variation in
distances, p = 0.15, on two different distance metrics, with equal dispersion,
with and without the QC-flagged sample. What composition *does* track here is
BV status (Nugent R2 = 0.24) — and the arms carry BV at similar rates.

Two honest caveats:

1. **This is not "proof of no difference".** With 39/28/26 people per arm we
   could only detect a fairly large difference. A real 3% difference would
   have been invisible here.
2. The composition-vs-BV analysis above suggests the more interesting Study B
   questions might be at the level of *which species* differ by arm
   (a DESeq2 question, another document), not whether the community as a
   whole shifts.

## How you could catch me being wrong

- **Count the points on the first ordination** by colour: 39 injectable, 28
  pill, 26 ring. If you see 471 points I accidentally loaded the instructional
  dataset.
- **Rerun the `permanova` chunk with `permutations = 9999`.** The p-value for
  arm should stay near 0.15; if it jumps to 0.03 or 0.5, something is wrong
  with my seed or model.
- **Replace `by = "margin"` with no `by` argument** (sequential terms): arm
  alone should still be around p = 0.15, because arm is the first term in the
  formula and enters first either way.
- **The shuffle plot is the check for the shuffle plot**: it has its own
  subtitle reporting how many shuffles beat the real R2. I claim about 4 of
  20 — if the subtitle says 0 of 20, my "no difference" verdict is weaker
  than I said.

## Choices made

- Bray-Curtis on compositional shares as the primary distance — alternative not chosen: Jaccard, which throws away abundance and keeps only presence/absence; Tuesday showed the dominance signal is what separates these communities.
- PERMANOVA (`adonis2`) as the primary test — alternative not chosen: ANOSIM, which only uses ranks of the distances and answers a slightly different question.
- `by = "margin"` with `rnaseq_batch` in the model — alternative not chosen: testing arm alone; I ran that too (p = 0.15, same verdict), and report both.
- `betadisper` + `permutest` before trusting PERMANOVA — alternative not chosen: skipping the dispersion check, which would have been unsafe; PERMANOVA cannot tell centre differences from spread differences on its own.
- Aitchison distance (CLR + Euclidean) as the robustness check — alternative not chosen: trusting one distance metric; I noted the CLR zero handling (add half the smallest nonzero count) rather than picking a different pseudocount.
- Pre-filtered never-observed species (`min_count = 1, min_samples = 1`) as primary — alternative not chosen: keeping all 220 species; I ran that as a sensitivity (same verdict).
- Kept the shallow `B006` in the primary analysis — alternative not chosen: dropping it up front; I dropped it in a robustness chunk instead (p = 0.11, same verdict).
- 999 permutations with `set.seed(2026)` — alternative not chosen: 99 permutations (p-values too coarse) or 9999 (slower, adds nothing).
- Shuffle-null of 20 shuffles at 99 permutations to picture the null — alternative not chosen: reading the p-value alone without a visual null.
- Coloured the ordination by `bv`/Nugent to show what a real signal looks like next to arm — alternative not chosen: colouring only by arm, which would have left the 33.8% axis unexplained.
- Tested the community question on the microbiome table only — alternative not chosen: the same pipeline on the RNAseq table, which answers a different question (gene expression, not community) and belongs in its own document.
